items.prompt: Two services both write to `orders.total` inside their own valid SQL transactions, and a lost update still lets an order exceed its credit limit. What does that show?
choices: SQL transactions don't actually guarantee atomicity
A transaction protects one write's atomicity, but has no idea which combined states are valid for your domain
The bug means neither service was using transactions correctly
This can only happen with a database that doesn't support isolation levels
items.explanation: Each write was atomic on its own — that's exactly what a transaction guarantees. What was missing was a rule enforced across the writes: 'total must never exceed the credit limit.' No transaction knows your business rules; only your model does.
items.reference:
No aggregate

Two writers read the same total, both compute independently, last write wins

Aggregate root

Every write re-checks the invariant against current state, inside one method

Why: a valid SQL transaction only guarantees one write is atomic — it says nothing about a rule that spans several rows at once.

items.prompt: Request A and Request B both read an order's total as $95 at the same instant, then each independently compute and write a new total. What kind of bug is this?
choices: A lost update — one writer's change is silently overwritten because neither read the other's in-flight change
A deadlock — both requests are blocked waiting on each other
A SQL injection vulnerability
A currency rounding error
items.explanation: This is a classic lost update: both writers computed their new value from the same stale snapshot, so whichever writes last wins and the other writer's change vanishes with no error raised anywhere.

Why: a valid SQL transaction only guarantees one write is atomic — it says nothing about a rule that spans several rows at once.

items.prompt: An order ships with 2 line items but a total that only reflects 1 of them, and the credit limit was never actually checked against the true total. What was the underlying design gap?
choices: No single place enforced 'total plus every added line must stay under the credit limit' on every write
The credit limit itself was set too low
The two services should have used the same programming language
The order table was missing a foreign key constraint
items.explanation: The gap wasn't a missing constraint on one table — it was that no single piece of code owned checking the combined invariant (total vs. credit limit) every time something changed it.

Why: a valid SQL transaction only guarantees one write is atomic — it says nothing about a rule that spans several rows at once.

items.prompt: What is an aggregate root's main job?
choices: Being the single entry point for changes to the cluster of objects it owns, checking invariants on every mutation
Storing the aggregate's data in a single database table
Formatting the aggregate's fields for display in an API response
Logging every read of the aggregate for auditing
items.explanation: The aggregate root is the gatekeeper: every change to any object inside the aggregate goes through one of its methods, and that's where invariants get checked, every time, with no other way in.
items.reference:
🚪 One entry point: the root's methods
🔒 Children (like OrderLine) are never edited directly from outside
✅ Invariants checked inside every mutating method

Why: if anything outside the aggregate can mutate a child directly, the root's invariant checks are just one of several ways in — and the cheapest one to accidentally bypass wins.

choices: Because OrderLine objects are read-only by the database
Because that would bypass Order's invariant checks entirely — the whole point of routing changes through the root
Because OrderLine doesn't have a setQuantity method in any language
Because quantities can only be set when the order is first created
items.explanation: If anything outside the aggregate can mutate a child object directly, the root's invariant-checking methods become optional rather than mandatory — and the shortest path through the code wins over the safe one.

items.prompt: Which of these best describes an 'aggregate' as DDD uses the term?
choices: A cluster of objects that must be treated as one consistency unit because a business rule spans more than one of them
Any group of database tables that are joined together in a query
A cached, denormalized read model used for reporting
A microservice that owns more than one REST endpoint
items.explanation: An aggregate is a modeling decision, not a database or infrastructure concept — it's about which objects have to be checked together, every time, because at least one rule depends on more than one of them at once.

items.prompt: `OrderLine #7`'s quantity changes from 2 to 3. Is it still considered line 7, or a new object?
choices: Still line 7 — its identity persists across the change, which is what makes it an entity
A new object — any change to its fields creates a different line
It depends on whether the database assigns a new primary key
Neither — OrderLine has no identity at all
items.explanation: An entity's defining trait is that its identity survives changes to its other fields. Line 7 stays line 7 even after its quantity changes — that's exactly what makes it an entity rather than a value object.
items.reference:
Entity

Has identity; same thing even after it changes (OrderLine #7 stays #7)

Value object

No identity; compared by content only (two $10s are just equal)

Why: the question to ask is "does WHICH ONE matter, or only WHAT IT EQUALS" — that answer decides identity vs. value.

items.prompt: Two separate `Money($10)` objects exist in the system. Are they 'the same one' or just equal?
choices: Just equal — value objects have no identity, they're compared purely by their contents
The same one — there can only be one instance of any given amount
It depends on which one was created first
Neither — Money objects can't be compared at all
items.explanation: Value objects are interchangeable by design: you never ask 'which $10 is this, specifically,' only 'does this amount equal that one.' That's the whole distinction from an entity.

items.prompt: What does a repository do in this pattern?
choices: It's the only door in and out of an aggregate's storage — it loads and saves whole aggregates, never a lone child object
It's a folder in the codebase where all the domain classes live
It's a caching layer that sits in front of the database for performance
It converts domain objects into HTML for rendering
items.explanation: A repository's defining feature here isn't caching or performance — it's that it only exposes whole-aggregate operations, closing off any path that would let code save a child object without going through the root.
items.reference:
📦 save(order) — the WHOLE aggregate, every time
🚫 No OrderLineRepository — that door doesn't exist
🔍 findById(id) returns the whole aggregate too

Why: a repository that could save a single child object would let code bypass the aggregate root's invariant checks entirely.

Because OrderLine data doesn't actually need to be persisted
Because a repository can only exist for the very first class defined in a file
Because OrderLine and Order must always share a single database table
items.explanation: The absence is deliberate: exposing a repository for a child object would recreate exactly the bug from L1 — a write path that skips the aggregate root's invariant checks entirely.

items.prompt: What is a domain event, in this pattern?
choices: A record, raised from inside the aggregate root, of something that actually happened — published for other parts of the system to react to
A log line written to a monitoring dashboard
A scheduled cron job that runs periodic maintenance
A validation error returned to the caller when an invariant is violated
items.explanation: A domain event captures something the aggregate root decided genuinely happened (like OrderPlaced) — it's raised from inside the aggregate, then published afterward so other contexts can react without the aggregate calling them directly.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Order.placeOrder() records OrderPlaced internally
2️⃣ repository.save(order) commits
3️⃣ only THEN: pullDomainEvents() + publish

Why: publishing before commit risks telling other contexts about a change that then fails to persist.

items.prompt: Why doesn't `Order.placeOrder()` just call Billing's API directly instead of raising a domain event?
choices: Calling Billing directly would couple Order to Billing's availability and shape — exactly what bounded contexts exist to avoid
Because Order objects aren't allowed to make network calls under any circumstances
Because Billing's API doesn't accept order data in any format
Because domain events are faster than API calls, and that's the only reason to prefer them
items.explanation: If Order called Billing directly, Order would depend on Billing's uptime and API shape. Raising an event and letting Billing subscribe keeps that dependency one-directional and optional from Order's side.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Order.placeOrder() records OrderPlaced internally
2️⃣ repository.save(order) commits
3️⃣ only THEN: pullDomainEvents() + publish

Why: publishing before commit risks telling other contexts about a change that then fails to persist.

items.prompt: At what point should a domain event actually be published to the rest of the system?
choices: After the aggregate's own change has successfully been saved, not before
The instant the event is recorded inside the aggregate root's method
Only once a day, in a scheduled batch
Before the save, so downstream systems can veto the change
items.explanation: Publishing before the save commits risks telling other contexts about a change that then fails to persist. Publishing only after a successful save keeps the event trustworthy — if it was published, it's true.

items.prompt: A single SQL transaction guarantees a write is atomic. Why isn't that enough to prevent an aggregate's invariant from being violated?
choices: Atomicity only protects one write from being partially applied — it says nothing about what combination of values across multiple writes is actually valid for your domain
SQL transactions are inherently unreliable and randomly fail
Atomicity and consistency are the same guarantee, so this shouldn't be possible
Because transactions only work within a single table
items.explanation: A transaction's guarantee is narrow and mechanical: this one write either fully happens or doesn't. Nothing about that tells the database which combined states are meaningful — that has to come from code that models the rule explicitly.
items.reference:
⚛️ Transaction = one write is all-or-nothing
🧩 Aggregate = which objects must stay consistent WITH EACH OTHER

Why: a transaction has no idea what your business rules are — only your model, expressed as an aggregate boundary, does.

items.prompt: Why is an aggregate boundary described as a 'modeling decision' rather than a database concept?
choices: Because it's chosen based on which business rules span multiple objects at once, not based on how tables happen to be structured
Because aggregates only exist in NoSQL databases
Because the database schema always dictates the aggregate boundary automatically
Because it's an arbitrary choice with no consequences either way
items.explanation: The boundary is drawn around 'the smallest cluster of objects that must be consistent with each other on every write' — a decision about the domain's rules, which a schema can support but doesn't determine on its own.

Nothing — validating at the end is equivalent to validating on every step

The domain event would fire twice

Because a single aggregate can never reference more than one other object
Because Order doesn't need any information about the customer at all

There would be no cost — the two models are functionally identical

items.prompt: In the sequence diagram, `pullDomainEvents()` is called by the application layer, not from inside `placeOrder()` itself. Why keep that split?

items.prompt: Two teams in the same company: Team B's context depends on Team A's model, and Team B can file requests that influence Team A's roadmap. Which context-mapping pattern is this?
choices: Customer-supplier — both answer to the same organization, so downstream's needs can feed upstream's priorities
Conformist — downstream must adopt whatever upstream provides with no influence
Shared kernel — both teams jointly own a single piece of the model
Anticorruption layer — this describes a translation technique, not a relationship type
items.explanation: Customer-supplier specifically describes a relationship where the downstream team has real standing to prioritize its needs against the upstream team's backlog — something only possible when both report to the same organization.
items.reference:
Customer-supplier

Same org, downstream's needs feed upstream's backlog

Open host service

One stable published contract for many consumers, instead of N bespoke ones

Why: misreading which pattern actually governs a relationship means either filing requests nobody will act on, or building a translation layer nobody needed.

items.prompt: A context is consumed by many different downstream teams, each with slightly different needs. What does an open host service / published language do about that?
choices: Exposes one stable, versioned contract for everyone, instead of building a bespoke integration per consumer
Forces every downstream team to build their own anticorruption layer against a different private API
Merges all the downstream teams into a single bounded context
Requires every consumer to poll the database directly instead of using an API
items.explanation: Open host service / published language trades N custom integrations for one shared, stable contract — worthwhile specifically when many consumers need the same upstream data, rather than one bespoke relationship at a time.

items.prompt: Implement `Money.equals(other)` so two Money instances with the same amount and currency are considered equal, using cents internally to avoid floating point drift.

tests.description: equal dollar amounts compare equal
tests.expr: expect(Money.fromDollars(10).equals(Money.fromDollars(10))).toBe(true)

tests.description: different amounts compare unequal
tests.expr: expect(Money.fromDollars(10).equals(Money.fromDollars(10.01))).toBe(false)

tests.description: different currencies compare unequal even with same amount

items.explanation: Comparing integer cents (not floating-point dollars) avoids rounding drift across repeated arithmetic, and comparing both cents and currency is what makes equals() actually mean 'the same value,' the defining trait of a value object.

tests.expr: const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: "o1", total: 100 }); repo.save({ id: "o1", total: 200 }); expect(repo.findById("o1").total).toBe(200)

items.explanation: save() and findById() are the only two operations exposed — there is deliberately no method that touches anything smaller than a whole Order, which is what keeps the repository from becoming a bypass around the aggregate root.
items.reference:
📦 save(order) — the WHOLE aggregate, every time
🚫 No OrderLineRepository — that door doesn't exist
🔍 findById(id) returns the whole aggregate too

Why: a repository that could save a single child object would let code bypass the aggregate root's invariant checks entirely.

items.prompt: Extend `InMemoryOrderRepository.save(order)` to throw a `ConcurrencyConflictError` if the stored order's `version` doesn't match the incoming order's `version` (optimistic concurrency).

tests.description: first save of a new order succeeds
tests.expr: const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: "o1", version: 0 }); expect(repo.findById("o1").version).toBe(1)

tests.description: saving with a stale version throws
tests.expr: const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: "o1", version: 0 }); expect(() => repo.save({ id: "o1", version: 0 })).toThrow()

tests.description: saving with the current version succeeds
tests.expr: const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: "o1", version: 0 }); repo.save({ id: "o1", version: 1 }); expect(repo.findById("o1").version).toBe(2)

items.explanation: This is the actual fix for the lost-update race from L1: rejecting a save whose version is stale turns a silent overwrite into a visible error the caller must reload and retry against.
items.reference:
📖 Both writers read version 1
✅ First save succeeds → store moves to version 2
❌ Second save still carries version 1 → rejected, must reload

Why: rejecting the stale write turns a silent lost update into a visible signal to reload and retry against current reality.

items.prompt: Implement `Order.placeOrder()` to push an `{ type: "OrderPlaced", orderId }` event onto `this.pendingEvents`, and `pullDomainEvents()` to drain and return them.

tests.description: placeOrder records an event
tests.expr: const o = new Order("o1"); o.placeOrder(); expect(o.pullDomainEvents().length).toBe(1)

tests.description: the event has the right shape
tests.expr: const o = new Order("o1"); o.placeOrder(); expect(o.pullDomainEvents()[0].type).toBe("OrderPlaced")

tests.description: pulling drains the events — a second pull is empty
tests.expr: const o = new Order("o1"); o.placeOrder(); o.pullDomainEvents(); expect(o.pullDomainEvents().length).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Draining (returning, then clearing) rather than just returning a reference is what prevents the same event from being re-published if pullDomainEvents() is accidentally called twice.
items.reference:
➕ record() pushes onto a private pendingEvents array
🚰 pullDomainEvents() drains it and returns the events
🧹 Called once, right after a successful save

Why: draining rather than peeking prevents the same event from being published twice if pullDomainEvents() is called again.

items.prompt: Extend `Order` so `addLine()` does NOT raise any event (only `placeOrder()` should), even though both methods mutate the aggregate.

tests.description: addLine alone raises no events
tests.expr: const o = new Order("o1"); o.addLine(10); expect(o.pullDomainEvents().length).toBe(0)

tests.description: placeOrder still raises exactly one event
tests.expr: const o = new Order("o1"); o.addLine(10); o.placeOrder(); expect(o.pullDomainEvents().length).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Not every mutation is a domain event — only the ones another context genuinely needs to react to. Raising an event on every internal change would flood subscribers with noise nobody asked for.
items.reference:

🚰 pullDomainEvents() drains it and returns the events
🧹 Called once, right after a successful save

Why: draining rather than peeking prevents the same event from being published twice if pullDomainEvents() is called again.

items.prompt: Implement `pullDomainEvents()` to include an `occurredAt` timestamp field (any Date) on each event pushed by `placeOrder()`.

items.explanation: A timestamp on the event itself (not just on the row it might get persisted to) means any subscriber can reason about ordering and staleness without a round trip back to the aggregate that raised it.

items.prompt: Implement `LegacyInventoryAdapter.toStockAvailability(row)` translating a legacy `{ qty_on_hand: string, stat: "A"|"B"|"D" }` row into `{ availableQuantity: number, canFulfill: boolean }`. `canFulfill` is true only when stat is "A" and quantity is greater than 0.

tests.description: active with stock can fulfill
tests.expr: expect(new LegacyInventoryAdapter().toStockAvailability({ qty_on_hand: "5", stat: "A" }).canFulfill).toBe(true)

tests.description: active with zero stock cannot fulfill
tests.expr: expect(new LegacyInventoryAdapter().toStockAvailability({ qty_on_hand: "0", stat: "A" }).canFulfill).toBe(false)

tests.description: backordered cannot fulfill even with a positive quantity string
tests.expr: expect(new LegacyInventoryAdapter().toStockAvailability({ qty_on_hand: "5", stat: "B" }).canFulfill).toBe(false)

tests.description: availableQuantity is parsed as a number, not left as a string
tests.expr: expect(new LegacyInventoryAdapter().toStockAvailability({ qty_on_hand: "5", stat: "A" }).availableQuantity).toBe(5)

items.explanation: The adapter is the one place that knows the legacy field names and status codes exist at all — everything downstream of it only ever sees the clean, domain-owned StockAvailability shape.
items.reference:
🏚️ Legacy shape: qty_on_hand (string), stat (A/B/D)
🔁 Adapter translates it into StockAvailability
🧼 Order never imports the legacy shape

Why: if the vendor renames a field, exactly one file — the adapter — has to change.

items.prompt: The legacy system was updated: discontinued items now report stat "D" but sometimes still have a nonzero qty_on_hand (leftover warehouse stock not for sale). Update `toStockAvailability` so discontinued items are never fulfillable, regardless of quantity.

tests.description: active with stock can fulfill
tests.expr: expect(new LegacyInventoryAdapter().toStockAvailability({ qty_on_hand: "5", stat: "A" }).canFulfill).toBe(true)

tests.description: discontinued with leftover stock cannot fulfill
tests.expr: expect(new LegacyInventoryAdapter().toStockAvailability({ qty_on_hand: "5", stat: "D" }).canFulfill).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Because Order only ever depends on the adapter's output shape, absorbing this legacy quirk (discontinued-but-in-stock) took a one-line change in a single file — nothing in Order's own model had to change at all.
